newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian president vows to find 1989 revolt truth.
newsitem.headline: Romanian president vows to find 1989 revolt truth.

text.p: Romanian President Emil Constantinescu promised on Monday to uncover the facts behind hundreds of unexplained deaths in the revolt seven years ago that toppled Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

Constantinescu told 15,000 demonstrators marking the outbreak of the 1989 upheaval that Romania's new leaders had a duty to investigate allegations that Communists sowed confusion and caused deaths after Ceausescu's execution in order that they could hang on to power.

"We will find out the truth. We will find out who shot people between December 16 and 22 and later," Constantinescu said from the balcony where leaders of the revolt addressed crowds for three days in mid-December 1989.
"There will be no shooting of people in our country. Let us show Europe and the world that Romania is a country based on honesty, understanding and hard work."
Constantinescu, who ousted former Communist Ion Iliescu in elections last month, was cheered by demontrators who chanted "The truth, the truth!" and "Who was shooting at us?"

Constantinescu came to power on pledges to reverse a plunge in living standards which has left Romania well behind ex-communist Poland and Hungary and to root out corruption he said was endemic in the former government.
The 1989 revolt was Eastern Europe's bloodiest overturn of Communist rule with more than 1,000 killed in over a week of clashes with security forces.

The events, which came after the downfall of Communism throughout most of Eastern Europe, were sparked in Timisoara on December 15, when hundreds of protesters set up a vigil to protect the church of an ethnic Hungarian priest accused of dissident activity.

The demonstration in the city near the Yugoslav border, which has large Serb, German and Hungarian minorities, quickly swelled the next day with tens of thousands of people filling the theatre square.
Security forces killed 119 people and wounded hundreds, many desperately seeking refuge in a locked Orthodox cathedral.

The role of Communists in Ceausescu's downfall became a major election issue. Constantinescu openly demanded an explanation why hundreds of people were shot dead after Ceausescu had fled the capital on December 22.
Ceausescu was summarily tried and executed on Christmas Day.

Liberals allege that Communists spread rumours of terrorist attacks in Bucharest and other cities. Although dozens of top Communists were jailed for their role in suppressing the revolt, all have since been set free.
Former Communists deny the charges and describe the events launched in Timisoara as a revolt born of popular anger.

Iliescu, reproached for never visiting Timisoara on the December anniversary during his six years in office, sent a message to the city's residents on Monday saying the revolution was the outcome of the people's political will and not a coup.
The liberals viewed the rout of Iliescu and his party of ex-Communists in both presidential and general polls as the crowning of what they said was an unfinished 1989 revolution.
Many of Monday's marchers carried national flags with holes in the middle as they did in 1989 after ripping out the crest of Communist Romania.
